# Jessica Kendall-Bar | ART + SCIENCE
marine biologist & science communicator

## Welcome
My research combines engineering, data science, ecology, and visualization to measure behavior and physiology of marine animals in a changing climate. For my dissertation, I developed a non-invasive system to record and visualize the sleep patterns of seals at sea published in Science.

## An Interdisciplinary Approach

### Design
Engineer new biosensors.

### Visualize
See invisible behavior and physiology.

### Apply
Models to go from individuals to ecosystems.

### Communicate
Science communication to maximize impact.

## Sleep at sea
As increasing human impact coincides with changing ecosystems, it is important to assess how our activities affect animals' natural behavior. Marine mammal sleep had only been studied in the lab. For my dissertation, I combined art, engineering, and biology to develop a system to monitor and visualize the sleep patterns of seals at sea. These tools allow us to learn more about where, when, and how animals sleep at sea so that we can better manage and protect their critical resting habitats.

### Design
I designed a surface-mounted system for non-invasive recordings of sleep at sea.

Kendall-Bar et al. Eavesdropping on the Brain at Sea. Animal Biotelemetry (2022).

### Visualize
I designed a visualization toolbox to allow us to see behavior alongside neurological state.

Kendall-Bar et al. Visualizing Life in the Deep. IEEE VIS (2021).

### Apply
I applied EEG-derived sleep patterns of wild seals to interpret sleep patterns at the population level.

Kendall-Bar et al. Brain activity of diving seals. Science (2023).

## Science Communication & Data Visualization
Videos, animations, public lectures, maps, and infographics that use data, art, and underwater cinematography to tell stories about science.

# About
Dr. Jessica Kendall-Bar is a Schmidt AI in Science Postdoctoral Fellow at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego. Her research combines engineering, data science, ecology, and visualization to measure behavior and physiology of marine animals amidst a changing climate. For her dissertation, she developed a non-invasive system to record and visualize the first recordings of marine mammal sleep at sea published in Science.

She is an award-winning scientist, artist, and science communicator who designs data visualization courses, large-scale exhibits, immersive analytical tools, and decision support tools. Her data visualizations, published in local news outlets, The New York Times, and The Atlantic, have informed international policy in domains ranging from marine mammal conservation to coral reef restoration.

See Jessica's Google Scholar profile.

title: Sleep at Sea
summary: Science 2023 sleep-at-sea page with explainer graphics, press links, and key findings.
body:
# Sleep at Sea
Brain activity of diving seals reveals short sleep cycles at depth.

## Dive into the study
- Science paper
- ResearchGate PDF
- See visualizations
- See press coverage

Read coverage by Science, CNN, NPR, BBC, The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Washington Post, and National Geographic.

When you imagine a sleeping seal, you might think of a seal sleeping on the beach or bobbing in shallow water. You might have seen videos of harbor seals floating in the kelp as they sleep, but what about when a northern elephant seal spends 8 months at sea in search of food, traveling over 10,000 km?

Dolphins and fur seals can sleep in half of their brain at a time allowing them to monitor predators while they sleep, but a true seal, like an elephant seal or a harbor seal, sleeps just like us, shutting off their brain completely.

Our new study, recently published in Science, shares just how little seals sleep at sea in the first recordings of sleep for a wild marine mammal. We equipped northern elephant seals with sleep monitors as they dove in the deep Monterey canyon to find that they sleep in short naps deep below the ocean’s surface.

They dive down, start to glide, their brain waves sync up into large slow waves. Then, they transition to REM sleep where they flip upside down and spin a circle, falling like a leaf. Seals sleeping in the open ocean were upside down 100% of REM sleep time, suggesting that just like us, they become paralyzed during REM.

Sleeping at sea not only means they’re vulnerable to predation, but they’re also missing out on foraging opportunities. Seals slept around 10 hours a day on land, but limited sleep to less than 2 hours a day while at sea.

Using the long-term, 20-year elephant seal dataset curated by the Costa lab at UC Santa Cruz, we developed an algorithm that estimates sleep from time-depth records with 93% accuracy. We analyzed over 3 million dives, identifying over 500,000 sleeping dives for 334 seals on trips lasting up to 295 days.

Across several months at sea, elephant seals averaged only 2 hours of sleep per day, exhibiting unparalleled flexibility in sleep duration and rivaling the record for the least sleep among mammals.

By learning more about where, when, and how animals sleep at sea, we can improve the management and protection of their critical resting habitats.

## Citation
Kendall-Bar, JM; Williams, TM; Mukherji, R; Lozano, DA; Pitman, JK; Holser, RR; Keates, T; Beltran, RS; Robinson, PW; Crocker, DE; Adachi, T; Lyamin, OI; Vyssotski, AL; Costa, DP (2023). Brain activity of diving seals reveals short sleep cycles at depth. Science. Online at https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adf0566

title: Lightscapes of Fear
summary: Interactive map/explainer for female northern elephant seal behavioral rest and risk/reward tradeoffs.
body:
# Lightscapes of Fear
Behavioral Rest at Sea

This interactive map displays the tracks, trip duration, and dive metadata for 8 of the 71 female northern elephant seals incorporated in a study investigating the risk-reward tradeoffs of behavioral rest at sea.

Data from time-depth recorder and satellite instruments were processed in MATLAB and converted into KML files. Individual KML files were imported into a single KMZ zipped file to be imported into Google Maps' My Maps tool. Metadata was exported from MATLAB into a CSV and paired to the data layer containing each respective animal's track.

This interactive data visualization was created to accompany the Science Advances publication "Lightscapes of Fear: How mesopredators balance starvation and predation in the open ocean."

Map, infographics, and cover art by Jessica Kendall-Bar. Data analysis by Roxanne Beltran. Illustrations by Danielle Dube, Art-Science Residency with the Norris Center for Natural History.

## Pick a Seal
Click on a female northern elephant seal's track in the interactive map to learn her TOPPID, trip duration, departure date, arrival date, number of rest dives, and total number of dives.

## Follow Her Journey
While at sea, elephant seals perform transit dives, benthic dives, foraging dives, and drift dives. Drift dives are dives where they swim down to 200–300 meters, turn upside down, and drift for several minutes before swimming back to the surface.

As the seal gains body fat, her body composition shifts and she becomes less dense. Once she gains enough fat to become positively buoyant, she starts to float up toward the surface instead of sinking to the safety of darkness. She shifts her sleep schedule earlier so she can sleep in darkness, sacrificing valuable hours of nighttime foraging. She also begins her drift dives deeper so she ends at about the same depth as if negatively buoyant. By tracking buoyancy over time, the study tracks risk-taking behavior over months at sea.

# Undergraduate Research
UC Berkeley

## Marine Mammal Sleep Studies in Russia — Summer 2016
Eye State and Unihemispheric Sleep in the Northern Fur Seal. Advisor: Oleg Lyamin, Center for Sleep Research, UCLA School of Medicine.

I spent two months in Russia studying sleep in marine mammals, including northern fur seals and beluga whales. For my honors thesis, I focused on the correlation between eye state and sleep state, scored using both qualitative visual scoring and quantitative scoring based on spectral power analysis of EEG data.

Publication: Kendall-Bar, J.M., Mukhametov, L.M., Siegel, J.M., Lyamin, O.I. (2016). Eye state asymmetry during aquatic unihemispheric slow wave sleep in northern fur seals (Callorhinus ursinus). PLoS ONE 14(5): e0217025. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0217025.

## Pilot Whale Photo Identification — Summer 2015
Movement and occurrence of pilot whales. Advisors: Jay Barlow and Dave Weller, Southwest Fisheries Science Center NOAA. At NOAA’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center in La Jolla, I created a photo-identification catalog, conducted an analysis of matches, and compiled a short note published in Aquatic Mammals.

## Moorean Morays — Fall 2014
Behavior and den fidelity in moray eels on Moorea. I characterized moray eel behavior using a tailored ethogram and formulated behavioral comparisons across groups of morays, with attention to temporal, tidal, and weather patterns.

## Chemical Oceanography Research Cruises — August 2016, January 2013, October 2012
Aboard the RV Oceanus, RV Point Sur, and RV New Horizon. Advisor: Jim Bishop, UC Berkeley. I deployed carbon-profiling robots, CTD sensors, plankton nets, sediment PIT traps, McClane pumps, filtered ocean water samples for particulate inorganic carbon, filmed and analyzed diel vertical migration of zooplankton, and served as photographer/videographer for Lawrence Berkeley National Lab's Oceanbots blog.

## Sexual Selection in the Maritime Earwig — Summer 2014
Advisor: Vikram K. Iyengar, Villanova University. Publication: Kendall-Bar, J.M., Iyengar, V.K. (2016). Sexual selection by the seashore: the roles of body size and weaponry in mate choice and competition in the maritime earwig (Anisolabis maritima). Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology.

## Octopus Behavior Research — 2013–2014
Feeding behavior and repeated drill locations in shells.

## Internship at The Marine Mammal Center — Summer 2013
Video internship documenting patient care, surgeries, necropsies, releases, rescues, and instructional volunteer videos.

## Water Quality Testing for Surfrider LA — 2009–2012
Teach and Test program at Santa Monica High School; club water quality testing and first-flush response.

# Art for SciComm
Online learning portal for visualizing data to facilitate research, communication, and conservation.

## Data-Driven Animation for Science Communication
In this freely available MOOC, each student creates a scientific animation that tells a story with data to better communicate scientific results — learning programming, science writing, and technical animation skills.

This course trains students in data-based storytelling that promotes research and science communication for the benefit of communities and policymakers. Students draft a science writing script, create custom raster and vector graphics, data visualizations, and animations in Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator, Adobe After Effects, Adobe Premiere Pro, and Autodesk Maya. For their final project, students assemble these data-driven assets into an animated video abstract.

## Visualizing Life in the Deep
A creative pipeline for data-driven animations to facilitate marine mammal research, outreach, and conservation.

## Intro
Hello students, educators, and scientists! This page shares tools and techniques to visually communicate science and helps students, educators, and scientists navigate digital art for science communication.

## Terms of Use
Resources may contain unpublished data and are intended for educational purposes, not reproduction or redistribution. Please contact the site owner regarding copyright and use permissions or workshops.

## Workshops
- Animation in PowerPoint
- Animation in After Effects
- Animation in Maya
- Inkscape / Illustrator science illustration

# Data Visualization
The convergence of art, science, and technology for digital storytelling.

## Explore our 3D virtual gallery
This quarter I led a data visualization collective that brought together undergraduate and graduate students from Art: Games and Playable Media, Computational Media, Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, and Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Students worked with UCSC scientists to create graphical abstracts with custom graphics, publication-ready figures coded in R/Python/JavaScript, 2D and 3D animations, interactive websites, RShiny apps, ObservableHQ notebooks, and final projects combining course concepts.

## Final projects / student gallery
The gallery includes descriptions of each student’s project, the skills they learned, and links to websites/source code. Projects include hydrodynamical simulations of stars and black holes, human impacts on trophic activity patterns, bycatch in fisheries, Scott Creek fish passage, elephant seal census data, California ocean temperature projections, fur seal and sea lion isotopes, cryptic female choice simulations, drought effects on aquatic invertebrates, spring run Chinook salmon graphical abstracts, and Lightscapes of Fear.

body:
# Looking for Marla
The Story of a Fish's Transition.

## Support local bookstores
Bookshop Santa Cruz. After selling out last year, we've ordered 500 new books for you to stock up on. Order books now.

Interested in subsidized pricing or stocking our book at your institution? LookingForMarlaBook@gmail.com

Order through Bookshop Santa Cruz for local pick up or shipping.

## Donate
Don't need another book but want to support our project? This helps recuperate printing costs and allows us to start donating proceeds.

Looking for Marla follows the tale of a curious clownfish in transition as they find their way through fatherhood, and into motherhood. In wild clownfish populations, a male will transition into the role of the dominant female of the community when the female is removed. This biological fact is omitted from Finding Nemo and is a story that Looking for Marla helps to share and correct.

Looking for Marla hopes to inspire readers of all ages on their own journey of gender expression and self-exploration, while they discover the diversity of parental care strategies in the underwater world.

## About the creators
Meet Paloma, Audrey, & Jessie.

## Additional sections
- Motivation
- Buy your book
- Testimonials in support of Marla
- Sneak peek

## Audience note
This book is for educators, parents, youth, and anyone wanting to learn about sex and gender diversity in nature and gender pronouns in a fun way.

title: Animating the Ocean Biological Carbon Pump
summary: Carbon pump animation project with Nicolas Kendall-Bar and Exploratorium talk context.
body:
# Communicating Science: Animating the Ocean's Biological Carbon Pump
This is a project I worked on for about a year with my talented brother, Nicolas Kendall-Bar. I worked on the science and designs and my brother vividly brought it all to life. This complex process has been greatly simplified, but it demonstrates the incredible importance of the ocean in all of our lives.

The Exploratorium invited me to present this animation and other work on carbon chemistry in the ocean during their After Dark “Everything Matters: Tales of the Periodic Table” series. On March 16th 2017, I shared the recent findings of our research team with a room full of professors, advisors, friends, and members of the public. I enjoyed the challenge of creating a talk geared toward the general public that relied on powerful graphics and storytelling to communicate science.
